script.opening: "Morning. So I had a bit of a funny turn yesterday — the wife says I went stiff and shook for a minute and was a bit out of it after, but I feel totally fine now. I reckon it was just a faint, maybe I was tired. The main thing is — I drive for a living, so I just need you to confirm I'm okay to carry on driving, yeah? I can't afford any time off."

facts.text: You were sitting on the sofa watching TV about 9pm. You remember nothing until you "came round" on the floor with Kelly kneeling over you. You felt muddled for a while and then very sleepy.

facts.topic: What Kelly saw (if asked whether anyone saw it)
facts.text: "She says I went rigid, made a groaning noise, then my arms and legs were jerking for about a minute. My eyes were open. She timed it on her phone." Afterwards you did not know where you were for about 20 minutes.

You bit the side of your tongue — it is sore today. You had wet yourself. No warning beforehand — no light-headedness, sweating or feeling sick. You did not hit your head. No chest pain or palpitations before or after.

Sleeping badly for weeks — new baby, about 4 hours a night. You were drinking heavily at weekends ("10 or 12 pints Friday and Saturday") and stopped completely on Monday because you felt rough — the turn was on Wednesday. No drugs.
Never had anything like this. No head injuries, no febrile fits as a child that you know of. No family history of epilepsy. No family history of sudden death.
31, delivery driver for a parcel firm, driving a 3.5-tonne van on a normal car licence. You drove to the depot this morning. You are the only earner; Kelly is on maternity leave; you have a mortgage.
Losing your licence means losing your job. Deeper down: "My mate's brother has epilepsy and can't do anything." Reveal only if the doctor asks what worries you most.

Breezy and in a hurry at first, steering everything back to driving. If the doctor says plainly that this sounds like a seizure and that you must stop driving and tell the DVLA, argue once: "Can't you just put it down as a faint?" If they hold firm kindly, acknowledge the money worry and talk about what support exists, you become flat and quiet, then ask: "How long for?" Accept the plan.

ice.ideas: "It was just a faint because I was knackered."
ice.concerns: "If I can't drive I lose my job — and we've got a new baby and a mortgage."
ice.expectations: "Just confirm I'm okay to keep driving." You will accept honest advice if the doctor is clear and supportive.

cues: "I reckon it was just a faint." — say in the opening.
"I drive for a living." — say in the opening and again when driving is raised.
"Can't you just put it down as a faint?" — say once when DVLA is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Recognises this as a GENERALISED TONIC-CLONIC SEIZURE, not a faint — using the discriminating features (tonic-clonic movements ~1 min, lateral tongue-biting, incontinence, prolonged post-ictal confusion) — and does NOT accept the "just a faint" framing

Gives the clear, non-negotiable DRIVING advice: he MUST STOP DRIVING now and NOTIFY THE DVLA — a first seizure means a driving ban (typically 6 months for a car licence; far stricter/longer for Group 2/professional driving) — and does NOT provide false reassurance that he can keep driving

Identifies possible PROVOKING factors (sleep deprivation, alcohol use/withdrawal) and recognises that even a provoked seizure generally still carries driving restrictions and needs proper assessment — not dismissal

Arranges the WORK-UP: urgent referral to a first-seizure clinic / clinician with expertise in first seizures and diagnosing epilepsy, to be seen within 2 weeks (NICE NG217), a 12-lead ECG (to exclude a cardiac/arrhythmic cause of collapse; NICE CG109), bloods, and consideration of imaging/EEG per pathway; gives interim safety advice

Gives SAFETY advice meanwhile: avoid swimming/baths alone, working at heights/with dangerous machinery, and other situations where a seizure would be dangerous; address alcohol and sleep; what to do if another seizure occurs (and prolonged seizure >5 min → 999)

Handles the minimisation and the livelihood terror with honesty AND compassion: is firm and clear about the driving/DVLA duty while genuinely acknowledging the devastating impact on his job and income, and does not collude to keep him onside
Supports him through the blow — sick note, exploring work options/finances, the possibility of returning to driving after the relevant seizure-free period — so honesty doesn’t feel like abandonment

Safety-nets and documents: the explicit stop-driving/notify-DVLA advice given, first-seizure-clinic referral and ECG, interim safety advice, what to do if another/prolonged seizure occurs (999), and follow-up — the honest, supported plan, not false clearance

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang. I have to be straight with you though — from what your wife describes, this wasn’t a faint. Going stiff then shaking for a minute, biting the side of your tongue, wetting yourself, and being confused for twenty minutes afterwards — those are the features of a seizure, not a simple faint. I know that’s not what you wanted to hear."

"And I have to be honest about the driving, because it matters and I’d be failing you to fudge it: after a seizure, the law says you must stop driving and tell the DVLA. For a normal car licence that’s usually a six-month break; for driving professionally the rules are stricter. I can’t confirm you’re okay to drive — I’m really sorry, because I know what that means for your work."

"This is a genuine blow — your job, your income, the mortgage — and I’m not going to pretend otherwise or rush past it. Let’s deal with it properly: I’ll sort a sick note, we’ll look at your options at work and any support, and the important thing is this is very often temporary — many people drive again after the seizure-free period."

"There may be a reason this happened — you mentioned poor sleep and drinking heavily then stopping; both can trigger seizures. That doesn’t cancel the driving rules, but it matters for treatment. So I’m referring you urgently to a first-seizure clinic, doing a heart tracing to rule out a heart cause of the collapse, and some bloods."

"Until you’re assessed: don’t swim or bathe alone, avoid heights and dangerous machinery, and go easy on alcohol and get proper sleep. If you have another seizure, especially one lasting more than five minutes or back-to-back, that’s a 999. Your wife knowing what to do helps."

"I know I’ve given you hard news, and I’ve done it because being straight with you is the only way to keep you and others safe — imagine a seizure at the wheel. But I’m not leaving you to it: sick note, referral, support with work, and we’ll get you the answers. Notify the DVLA, stop driving for now, and come and see me so we can plan the next steps together."

f.learning: A "funny faint" with tonic-clonic movements lasting ~1 minute, LATERAL tongue-biting, urinary incontinence and prolonged post-ictal confusion is a GENERALISED TONIC-CLONIC SEIZURE, not a vasovagal faint (which is brief with quick full recovery and a trigger/prodrome). The non-negotiable examinable point is the DRIVING/DVLA duty: after a first seizure the patient MUST stop driving and notify the DVLA — usually 6 months seizure-free for a car (Group 1) licence after a first isolated unprovoked seizure (12 months if recurrence risk is higher) and far stricter, longer rules for Group 2/professional driving — so the patient cannot be "confirmed okay to drive", and even a provoked seizure generally still carries restrictions. Arrange the work-up (urgent referral to an epilepsy specialist/first-seizure clinic, seen within 2 weeks per NICE NG217, ECG to exclude a cardiac cause of collapse, bloods, imaging/EEG per pathway), identify provoking factors (sleep deprivation, alcohol use/withdrawal), and give interim safety advice (no swimming/baths alone, heights, machinery; 999 if a seizure >5 min). The hidden agenda is livelihood terror driving the minimisation; the skill is honesty AND compassion — be firm and clear about the driving duty while genuinely supporting the job/income blow (sick note, work options, the likely temporary nature) so honesty doesn’t feel like abandonment.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG217 (epilepsies, 2022, updated January 2025) · NICE CG109 (transient loss of consciousness) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive · GMC confidentiality guidance on fitness to drive (2017)
knowledge.summary: Tonic-clonic movements, a bitten tongue, incontinence and prolonged confusion describe a generalised seizure, not a faint. He must stop driving now and notify the DVLA, and needs an epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks.

points.t: Features favouring a seizure: stiffening then rhythmic jerking, a bitten side of the tongue, prolonged confusion afterwards, and incontinence. Syncope is usually brief with a trigger or prodrome and rapid recovery. A witness account is the key investigation; NICE CG109 asks for a 12-lead ECG in anyone with transient loss of consciousness.

NICE NG217: refer anyone with a suspected first seizure to an epilepsy specialist, to be seen within 2 weeks. In primary care: ECG, and bloods including glucose, electrolytes and calcium. Imaging, EEG, diagnosis and any anti-seizure medicine are specialist decisions.

DVLA: after a first isolated unprovoked seizure, a car or motorcycle licence is usually regained after 6 months seizure-free, or 12 months if investigations or clinical factors suggest a higher risk of recurrence. The time runs from the date of the seizure. The patient must stop driving and notify the DVLA; failing to notify can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.

Lorry and bus (Group 2) standards are much stricter — typically years off driving. The DVLA does not class a seizure linked to alcohol misuse or withdrawal as provoked: its alcohol-related seizure rules apply (Group 1 at least 6 months from the event), plus the misuse or dependence standards if relevant. The DVLA, not the GP, decides — he still stops and notifies.

Explore sleep deprivation, alcohol (including stopping suddenly after heavy use) and drugs. Interim advice: no swimming or bathing alone (shower instead), no working at heights or with dangerous machinery. Call 999 if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures repeat without recovery (NICE NG217).

GMC confidentiality guidance (2017): advise the patient of the legal duty and record it. If he continues to drive when not fit, make every reasonable effort to persuade him; if he still drives, inform the DVLA medical adviser, telling him first.

dg.d: Open question; acknowledged the driving agenda but gathered the story first.
Job as a delivery driver, sole income, mortgage, sleep and alcohol.
12-lead ECG and bloods (glucose, electrolytes, calcium); specialist to decide on imaging and EEG.
Generalised seizure versus syncope or cardiac arrhythmia; provoked (alcohol withdrawal, sleep loss) versus unprovoked.
Screened for head injury, focal deficit, fever or meningism, cardiac symptoms; 999 if seizure 5 minutes or more.
Stated clearly that this was a seizure, not a faint, without labelling it epilepsy.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop driving now and notify the DVLA; epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks; no anti-seizure medicine started in primary care.
Alcohol and sleep addressed with an offer of support; fit note and work options.
Interim safety advice, 999 threshold, documentation of driving advice, same-day review for ECG.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “just a faint” and “I can’t afford time off” as minimisation driven by fear, and explored it.
Idea (a faint from tiredness), concerns (licence, job, income, an epilepsy label), expectation (to be cleared to drive).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "If I can't drive I lose my job — and we've got a new baby and a mortgage." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Connor Healy? It’s Dr Ahmed from the surgery. You rang about something that happened yesterday — tell me about it in your own words.

Bit of a funny turn. The wife says I went stiff and shook for a minute and was out of it after, but I feel totally fine now. Probably just a faint — I was tired. Main thing is, I drive for a living, so I just need you to confirm I’m okay to carry on.
I hear that the driving is the big thing for you, and I promise we’ll talk about it properly. First I need to understand what happened, so I give you the right answer. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges his agenda and sets the order of the call

model.text: Go on then.
What were you doing just before, and do you remember any warning — feeling hot, sick, light-headed, or a strange feeling?
model.why: Explores prodrome and trigger to separate syncope from seizure

model.text: Nothing really. I don’t remember it happening. Next thing I knew I was on the floor and she was shaking me.
What did your wife say she saw, and how long were you muddled afterwards? Did you bite your tongue or wet yourself?
model.why: Obtains the witness account and discriminating features

model.text: She said I went stiff, then all my arms and legs jerked for about a minute. I bit the side of my tongue — still sore. And yeah, I’d wet myself. I was dopey for about twenty minutes.
Thank you for being honest about that. Has anything like this ever happened before? And how have you been sleeping, and what about alcohol lately?
Never before. Sleep’s been rubbish. I was drinking a fair bit, then I stopped a few days ago.
Any head injury in the fall, headache now, weakness, fever or stiff neck? Any palpitations or chest pain before it?
model.why: Screens for red flags needing emergency care and for a cardiac cause

model.text: No, nothing like that. Tongue’s sore, that’s all.
You said it was probably a faint. What would it mean for you if it turned out to be something else?
model.why: Explores the fear behind the minimisation

model.text: If I can’t drive, I can’t work. I’m the only one earning, there’s the mortgage. And I don’t want to be told I’ve got epilepsy.

That’s a lot riding on this, and I’m glad you told me. I have to be straight with you: going stiff, jerking all over, biting the side of your tongue, wetting yourself and being muddled for twenty minutes — that describes a seizure, not a faint. It doesn’t mean you have epilepsy; that’s for a specialist to decide.
model.why: Names the diagnosis honestly without premature labelling

model.text: So what does that mean for driving?

After a seizure, the law says you must stop driving from now and tell the DVLA yourself. For an ordinary car licence it’s usually six months without a further seizure, counted from yesterday. If you hold a lorry or bus licence, the rules are much longer. I can’t tell you you’re okay to drive — I’m sorry, because I know what that means.
model.why: Clear, non-negotiable DVLA advice with the correct Group 1 period

model.text: Six months? I’ll lose my job. Can’t you just not write it down?

I understand why you’d ask, and I can hear how frightening this is. But I can’t do that. If you had another seizure at the wheel, you or someone else could be killed. What I can do is help with everything that follows.
model.why: Declines collusion firmly but with empathy

model.text: I’m referring you to a specialist first-seizure clinic to be seen within two weeks. I’d like you in today for a heart tracing — sometimes a heart rhythm problem causes collapses — and blood tests. The alcohol and poor sleep may have triggered it, so that matters for the specialist too. Would you like help with the drinking?
model.why: NG217 referral, ECG and bloods, provoking factors, offer of alcohol support

model.text: Maybe. I’ll think about it.

That’s fair. On work: I can give you a fit note saying you’re not fit to drive but may be fit for other duties. It’s worth talking to your employer about non-driving work. And many people do get back to driving once the seizure-free period has passed.
model.why: Practical support for the livelihood impact so honesty isn’t abandonment

model.text: Okay. That’s something, I suppose.

Until you’re seen: shower rather than bath, don’t swim alone, avoid heights and dangerous machinery, try to keep regular sleep, and go steady with alcohol. If you have another seizure lasting five minutes or more, or one after another without waking, your wife should call 999.
model.why: Interim safety advice and the NG217 999 threshold

model.text: Can you tell me in your own words what you’re going to do about driving?
model.why: Teach-back on the key legal advice

model.text: Stop driving now, tell the DVLA, come in for the heart test, and wait for the clinic.
That’s right. I’ll record that we’ve discussed it, and I’ll see you today for the tracing so we can talk through the fit note together. I’m sorry this is such hard news.
model.why: Documents the advice and arranges follow-up

social.t: Loss of driving means loss of work for a delivery driver. Explore non-driving roles with his employer, and signpost benefits advice (Citizens Advice) if income stops.
Heavy drinking then stopping suddenly, plus poor sleep, may have triggered the seizure. Offer brief intervention and local alcohol services without judgement.

legal.t: The licence holder must notify the DVLA and stop driving. Group 1: usually 6 months seizure-free after a first isolated seizure (12 months if higher recurrence risk). Group 2: much longer. Failure to notify can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.
If a seizure disorder is diagnosed it may count as a disability, so his employer should consider reasonable adjustments such as non-driving duties. Access to Work may help.

professional.t: GMC guidance (2017): explain the duty to notify and record it. If he keeps driving against advice after reasonable efforts to persuade him, disclose to the DVLA medical adviser, telling him first.
A fit note can state “may be fit for work” with the adjustment “no driving”, keeping him in work where possible.

community.t: Epilepsy Action and Epilepsy Society offer information on first aid, driving and work, and helplines for patients and families.
Local community alcohol services and mutual-aid groups if he wants help cutting down safely.

redFlags: Head injury, persistent headache, focal weakness or failure to return to baseline — emergency assessment
Fever, neck stiffness or photophobia — possible CNS infection, 999
Palpitations, chest pain or exertional collapse — possible cardiac cause; ECG today
psychosocial: Occupation: delivery driver — sole earner, mortgage
Alcohol pattern (heavy then stopped) and poor sleep
Fear of an epilepsy label and what it means for his future
ice: Idea: “It was just a faint — I was tired”
Concern: losing his licence, his job and the family income; being told he has epilepsy
Expectation: to be told he can keep driving

playbook.diagnosis: A first generalised tonic-clonic seizure, possibly provoked by alcohol withdrawal and sleep loss: “What your wife saw describes a seizure, not a faint. It doesn’t mean you have epilepsy — a specialist will look at that — but it does mean you must stop driving for now.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A seizure is like an electrical storm in the brain — for a minute the signals fire all at once, which is why you went stiff and shook, and why you were muddled afterwards while the brain reset. A faint is different: the blood supply dips for a few seconds and you come round quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that losing your licence means losing your job and the mortgage. That’s a real fear, and I’ll help with it — but I can’t help by pretending this was a faint.”
management.psychosocial: Pair the hard news with concrete help: fit note for non-driving duties, conversation with his employer, benefits advice if needed, alcohol support, and the realistic prospect of driving again.
sharedPlan: Stop driving now; he notifies the DVLA; advice documented
Epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks (NICE NG217); ECG and bloods today
Alcohol and sleep advice with support offered; fit note
safetyNet: 999 if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures repeat without recovery
No bathing or swimming alone, no heights or dangerous machinery until assessed

pitfalls.intro: This station is a test of honesty under pressure. The clinical picture is clear; candidates fail by softening the driving advice, colluding with “just a faint”, or delivering the DVLA message so coldly that the patient disengages.

items.fail: Accepting the patient’s label of “a faint” without a witness history.
items.why: Tongue-biting, incontinence and 20 minutes of confusion point to a seizure. Missing them is a data-gathering fail.
items.fix: Ask what the witness saw, how long he was muddled, and about the tongue and incontinence.

items.fail: Vague driving advice — “best not to drive for a bit”.
items.why: The DVLA rules are specific and the patient must notify. Soft advice is a management and professionalism failure.
items.fix: “The law says you must stop driving from now and tell the DVLA. For a car licence it’s usually six months from yesterday.”

items.fail: Starting an anti-seizure medicine or ordering an MRI and EEG from primary care.
items.why: NICE NG217 places diagnosis and treatment with an epilepsy specialist.
items.fix: Refer to be seen within 2 weeks; do the ECG and bloods yourself.

items.fail: Agreeing to “not write it down” to keep the patient onside.
items.why: Collusion is dishonest and unsafe; examiners mark it as a serious professionalism concern.
items.fix: Refuse clearly and warmly, then move straight to what you can do to help.

items.fail: Giving the DVLA message and moving on without acknowledging the impact on his job.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Cold delivery drives non-adherence.
items.fix: Name the blow, then offer a fit note for non-driving duties, employer discussion and benefits advice.

items.fail: No interim safety advice or 999 threshold.
items.why: Drowning and injury are real risks before assessment; non-specific safety-netting is a common fail.
items.fix: Shower not bath, no swimming alone, no heights or machinery, 999 at 5 minutes.

items.fail: Not documenting or confirming that the driving advice was understood.
items.why: The advice has legal weight; unclear understanding leaves him and the public at risk.
items.fix: Teach-back — “What are you going to do about driving?” — and record it.

timeMap.d: He opens with the driving request. Acknowledge it and promise to return to it after hearing the story.
Prodrome, what his wife saw, duration, tongue, incontinence, recovery, previous events, sleep, alcohol, red flags.
Job, sole income, mortgage, fear of an epilepsy label.
Seizure not faint. Stop driving, notify DVLA. Refuse collusion kindly. Epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks, ECG, bloods, alcohol support, fit note.
Bath, swimming, heights, machinery. 999 at 5 minutes. Teach-back on driving. Document.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “just a faint”; tells him he can keep driving or leaves driving unmentioned; agrees not to record it; no specialist referral or ECG; no safety advice.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a seizure from the history; tells him clearly to stop driving and notify the DVLA; refers to an epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks; arranges ECG and bloods; gives interim safety advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: elicits his fear about income and an epilepsy label and responds to it; declines to collude while staying on his side; explores alcohol withdrawal as a trigger and offers support; offers a fit note for non-driving duties and explains that driving is often regained; uses teach-back and documents the advice.

avoid.dont: “It was probably just a faint — see how you go.”
avoid.instead: “What your wife saw describes a seizure, not a faint, and we need to take it seriously.”
avoid.why: Colluding with the minimisation misses the diagnosis and the legal duty.

avoid.dont: “I won’t put it in your notes, then.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t leave it out — but I can help with work, the fit note and getting you seen quickly.”
avoid.why: Concealment is dishonest and puts the public at risk.

avoid.dont: “You’ll have to tell the DVLA. Anything else?”
avoid.instead: “I know this is a huge blow. Let’s look at what we can do about work and money.”
avoid.why: Correct but cold advice fails the Relating domain and risks non-adherence.

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. I’ll think about it.

That’s fair. On work: I can give you a fit note saying you’re not fit to drive but may be fit for other duties. It’s worth talking to your employer about non-driving work. And many people do get back to driving once the seizure-free period has passed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical support for the livelihood impact so honesty isn’t abandonment

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s something, I suppose.

Until you’re seen: shower rather than bath, don’t swim alone, avoid heights and dangerous machinery, try to keep regular sleep, and go steady with alcohol. If you have another seizure lasting five minutes or more, or one after another without waking, your wife should call 999.
SCA_MODELS.why: Interim safety advice and the NG217 999 threshold

SCA_MODELS.text: Can you tell me in your own words what you’re going to do about driving?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back on the key legal advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Stop driving now, tell the DVLA, come in for the heart test, and wait for the clinic.
That’s right. I’ll record that we’ve discussed it, and I’ll see you today for the tracing so we can talk through the fit note together. I’m sorry this is such hard news.
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents the advice and arranges follow-up

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG217 (epilepsies, 2022, updated January 2025) · NICE CG109 (transient loss of consciousness) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive · GMC confidentiality guidance on fitness to drive (2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Tonic-clonic movements, a bitten tongue, incontinence and prolonged confusion describe a generalised seizure, not a faint. He must stop driving now and notify the DVLA, and needs an epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks.

points.t: Features favouring a seizure: stiffening then rhythmic jerking, a bitten side of the tongue, prolonged confusion afterwards, and incontinence. Syncope is usually brief with a trigger or prodrome and rapid recovery. A witness account is the key investigation; NICE CG109 asks for a 12-lead ECG in anyone with transient loss of consciousness.

NICE NG217: refer anyone with a suspected first seizure to an epilepsy specialist, to be seen within 2 weeks. In primary care: ECG, and bloods including glucose, electrolytes and calcium. Imaging, EEG, diagnosis and any anti-seizure medicine are specialist decisions.

DVLA: after a first isolated unprovoked seizure, a car or motorcycle licence is usually regained after 6 months seizure-free, or 12 months if investigations or clinical factors suggest a higher risk of recurrence. The time runs from the date of the seizure. The patient must stop driving and notify the DVLA; failing to notify can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.

Lorry and bus (Group 2) standards are much stricter — typically years off driving. The DVLA does not class a seizure linked to alcohol misuse or withdrawal as provoked: its alcohol-related seizure rules apply (Group 1 at least 6 months from the event), plus the misuse or dependence standards if relevant. The DVLA, not the GP, decides — he still stops and notifies.

Explore sleep deprivation, alcohol (including stopping suddenly after heavy use) and drugs. Interim advice: no swimming or bathing alone (shower instead), no working at heights or with dangerous machinery. Call 999 if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures repeat without recovery (NICE NG217).

GMC confidentiality guidance (2017): advise the patient of the legal duty and record it. If he continues to drive when not fit, make every reasonable effort to persuade him; if he still drives, inform the DVLA medical adviser, telling him first.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the driving agenda but gathered the story first.
Job as a delivery driver, sole income, mortgage, sleep and alcohol.
Picked up “just a faint” and “I can’t afford time off” as minimisation driven by fear, and explored it.
Idea (a faint from tiredness), concerns (licence, job, income, an epilepsy label), expectation (to be cleared to drive).
12-lead ECG and bloods (glucose, electrolytes, calcium); specialist to decide on imaging and EEG.
Generalised seizure versus syncope or cardiac arrhythmia; provoked (alcohol withdrawal, sleep loss) versus unprovoked.
Screened for head injury, focal deficit, fever or meningism, cardiac symptoms; 999 if seizure 5 minutes or more.
Stated clearly that this was a seizure, not a faint, without labelling it epilepsy.
Stop driving now and notify the DVLA; epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks; no anti-seizure medicine started in primary care.
Alcohol and sleep addressed with an offer of support; fit note and work options.
Interim safety advice, 999 threshold, documentation of driving advice, same-day review for ECG.

social.t: Loss of driving means loss of work for a delivery driver. Explore non-driving roles with his employer, and signpost benefits advice (Citizens Advice) if income stops.
Heavy drinking then stopping suddenly, plus poor sleep, may have triggered the seizure. Offer brief intervention and local alcohol services without judgement.

legal.t: The licence holder must notify the DVLA and stop driving. Group 1: usually 6 months seizure-free after a first isolated seizure (12 months if higher recurrence risk). Group 2: much longer. Failure to notify can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.
If a seizure disorder is diagnosed it may count as a disability, so his employer should consider reasonable adjustments such as non-driving duties. Access to Work may help.

professional.t: GMC guidance (2017): explain the duty to notify and record it. If he keeps driving against advice after reasonable efforts to persuade him, disclose to the DVLA medical adviser, telling him first.
A fit note can state “may be fit for work” with the adjustment “no driving”, keeping him in work where possible.

community.t: Epilepsy Action and Epilepsy Society offer information on first aid, driving and work, and helplines for patients and families.
Local community alcohol services and mutual-aid groups if he wants help cutting down safely.

redFlags: Head injury, persistent headache, focal weakness or failure to return to baseline — emergency assessment
Fever, neck stiffness or photophobia — possible CNS infection, 999
Palpitations, chest pain or exertional collapse — possible cardiac cause; ECG today
psychosocial: Occupation: delivery driver — sole earner, mortgage
Alcohol pattern (heavy then stopped) and poor sleep
Fear of an epilepsy label and what it means for his future
ice: Idea: “It was just a faint — I was tired”
Concern: losing his licence, his job and the family income; being told he has epilepsy
Expectation: to be told he can keep driving

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: A first generalised tonic-clonic seizure, possibly provoked by alcohol withdrawal and sleep loss: “What your wife saw describes a seizure, not a faint. It doesn’t mean you have epilepsy — a specialist will look at that — but it does mean you must stop driving for now.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A seizure is like an electrical storm in the brain — for a minute the signals fire all at once, which is why you went stiff and shook, and why you were muddled afterwards while the brain reset. A faint is different: the blood supply dips for a few seconds and you come round quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that losing your licence means losing your job and the mortgage. That’s a real fear, and I’ll help with it — but I can’t help by pretending this was a faint.”
management.psychosocial: Pair the hard news with concrete help: fit note for non-driving duties, conversation with his employer, benefits advice if needed, alcohol support, and the realistic prospect of driving again.

Epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks (NICE NG217); ECG and bloods today
Alcohol and sleep advice with support offered; fit note
safetyNet: 999 if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures repeat without recovery
No bathing or swimming alone, no heights or dangerous machinery until assessed

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is a test of honesty under pressure. The clinical picture is clear; candidates fail by softening the driving advice, colluding with “just a faint”, or delivering the DVLA message so coldly that the patient disengages.

items.fail: Accepting the patient’s label of “a faint” without a witness history.
items.why: Tongue-biting, incontinence and 20 minutes of confusion point to a seizure. Missing them is a data-gathering fail.
items.fix: Ask what the witness saw, how long he was muddled, and about the tongue and incontinence.

items.fail: Vague driving advice — “best not to drive for a bit”.
items.why: The DVLA rules are specific and the patient must notify. Soft advice is a management and professionalism failure.
items.fix: “The law says you must stop driving from now and tell the DVLA. For a car licence it’s usually six months from yesterday.”

items.fail: Starting an anti-seizure medicine or ordering an MRI and EEG from primary care.
items.why: NICE NG217 places diagnosis and treatment with an epilepsy specialist.
items.fix: Refer to be seen within 2 weeks; do the ECG and bloods yourself.

items.fail: Agreeing to “not write it down” to keep the patient onside.
items.why: Collusion is dishonest and unsafe; examiners mark it as a serious professionalism concern.
items.fix: Refuse clearly and warmly, then move straight to what you can do to help.

items.fail: Giving the DVLA message and moving on without acknowledging the impact on his job.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Cold delivery drives non-adherence.
items.fix: Name the blow, then offer a fit note for non-driving duties, employer discussion and benefits advice.

items.fail: No interim safety advice or 999 threshold.
items.why: Drowning and injury are real risks before assessment; non-specific safety-netting is a common fail.
items.fix: Shower not bath, no swimming alone, no heights or machinery, 999 at 5 minutes.

items.fail: Not documenting or confirming that the driving advice was understood.
items.why: The advice has legal weight; unclear understanding leaves him and the public at risk.
items.fix: Teach-back — “What are you going to do about driving?” — and record it.
